name: Mamluk Sultanate
summary: A state in Egypt and Syria ruled by a military caste of freed slave soldiers (mamluks). It stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260 and drove out the last Crusaders.

knownFor.label: Mamluk cavalry
knownFor.note: Slave-soldiers trained from childhood as elite horsemen.

knownFor.label: Battle of Ain Jalut
knownFor.note: The first major defeat of a Mongol army.

knownFor.label: Enamelled glass lamps
knownFor.note: Glass mosque lamps painted with enamel and gold.

knownFor.label: Mamluk Cairo
knownFor.note: Mosques, madrasas and tombs that still shape historic Cairo.

location.value: Egypt, Syria, Palestine and the Hejaz (including Mecca and Medina).
location.source: Wikipedia: Mamluk Sultanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

terrain.value: The Nile valley, the Levant coast and the Syrian desert.
terrain.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

climate.value: Arid; Egypt depended on the Nile flood.
climate.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

resources.value: Egyptian grain and the revenues of the spice trade.
resources.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

disasters.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

population.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

urbanisation.value: Cairo was one of the largest cities in the world.

disease.value: The Black Death killed a large share of Egypt’s people.
disease.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

migration.value: Mamluk soldiers were bought as boys from the steppe and the Caucasus.
migration.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

economicBase.value: Mainly agrarian, with large revenue from trade between Europe and the Indian Ocean.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Mamluk Sultanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

tradeRoutes.value: The spice trade from the Red Sea through Cairo and Alexandria to Venice and Genoa.
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: Mamluk Sultanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

moneyAndTax.value: Gold dinars and silver dirhams; Sultan Barsbay made the spice trade a state monopoly.
moneyAndTax.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

inequality.value: The iqta‘ system gave land revenues to mamluk officers.

governmentType.value: Rule by a military caste of freed slave soldiers (mamluks) under a sultan, with a ceremonial Abbasid caliph.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Mamluk Sultanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

keyRulers.value: Baybars (1260–1277), Qalawun, al-Nasir Muhammad, Qaitbay, Qansuh al-Ghuri.

succession.value: Usually by the strongest commander rather than by birth.
succession.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

institutions.value: The iqta‘ revenue system and a postal relay system (barid).
institutions.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

stability.value: Frequent coups: sultans were often deposed or killed by rival commanders.
stability.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

eliteConflict.value: Rival mamluk households (Bahri, then Burji Circassians) fought for power.
eliteConflict.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

armyAndTech.value: Elite cavalry trained from childhood in archery and horsemanship.
armyAndTech.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

majorWars.value: Defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260); conquered the Crusader states.

territoryChange.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

alliancesRivals.value: Allied with the Golden Horde; rivals of the Ilkhanate, the Crusaders and later the Ottomans.
alliancesRivals.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

inventions.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

scienceEducation.value: Madrasas, hospitals and scholars such as Ibn Khaldun (who worked in Cairo).
scienceEducation.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

openness.value: Reluctant to adopt firearms, which hurt them against the Ottomans.
openness.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

religion.value: Sunni Islam, with Christian and Jewish minorities.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Mamluk Sultanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

languageWriting.value: Arabic, with Kipchak Turkic and Circassian among the mamluks.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Mamluk Sultanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

artsArchitecture.value: Inlaid metalwork, enamelled glass, illuminated Qur’ans and Cairo’s Mamluk architecture.

socialStructure.value: Mamluk elite, scholars, merchants, townspeople and peasants.
socialStructure.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

sharedIdentity.value: Seen as defenders of Islam against the Mongols and Crusaders.
sharedIdentity.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

neighbours.value: The Ilkhanate, the Crusader states, the Ottomans and Ethiopia.
neighbours.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

ideasReligions.value: Cairo became the leading centre of Sunni scholarship after Baghdad fell in 1258.
ideasReligions.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

colonisation.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

riseSignals.value: Victory over the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260).
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Mamluk Sultanate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

peakPeriod.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

declineSignals.value: The Black Death and the loss of trade.
declineSignals.source: Irwin, The Middle East in the Middle Ages (1986)

sources.value: Mamluk chronicles. Checked against Wikipedia (“Mamluk Sultanate”).
